newsitem.title: CANADA: Funeral mogul Loewen fights back.
newsitem.headline: Funeral mogul Loewen fights back.

text.p: Ray Loewen, the indefatigable founder of North America's second-biggest mortuary and cemetery chain, has managed in the past year alone to save his company from bankruptcy and defeat a hostile takeover bid by his biggest competitor -- but his struggles are not over yet.

Instead, the 56-year-old former funeral director finds himself scrambling to regain the confidence of investors, keep profits growing and boost the price of shares in his once high-flying Loewen Group Inc.. His latest offensive kicks off Monday with a pitch to investors at a Smith Barney brokerage conference in New York and a whirlwind of media interviews.

"We have been under fire ... but we believe we are back to our traditional growth rate," Loewen said in an interview at the company's Vancouver headquarters before leaving for New York. "We have always prospered out of adversity ... and we're saying, 'Look what we can do now that the pressure is off.'"

That "pressure" included a brush with bankruptcy just a year ago after a Mississippi jury slapped the Loewen Group with a massive $500 million damage award in a breach-of-contract case. A last-minute, out-of-court settlement kept Loewen from filing for protection from creditors.

But a simultaneous collapse in its stock price made the 12-year-old company vulnerable to its chief rival, Houston-based Service Corp. International, which launched a $2.9 billion hostile bid for Loewen last autumn.
After fierce opposition from Loewen, Service dropped the offer in a surprise move earlier this month, saying it no longer felt its rival was worth the $43 a share it was offering.

"It was a big relief," Loewen said, leaning into a leather chair with his legs propped up after hip surgery. He learned of Service's decision to withdraw its bid from his hospital bed on Jan. 7, the day of his operation.
To celebrate the deal's demise, Loewen threw a bash at his mansion in a Vancouver suburb last week for elated staff members, investment bankers and advisers.

But the euphoria at Service's exit is tempered by the realisation that many shareholders are unhappy with the company's languishing stock price, analysts said. The stock price fell sharply on news of Service's withdrawal and is hovering around $36 on the New York Stock Exchange, well below its peak in the low 40s late last year during the takeover battle.
This stock price weakness could undermine Loewen's ability to make acquisitions, the source of its explosive growth, because it usually pays sellers of funeral homes and cemeteries with stock.
"A lot of shareholders are generally disappointed. The main issue right now is can they achieve the same value Service was offering and when?" said analyst Todd Richter of brokerage Dean Witter.
The company's chief contended the stock should be trading between about $42 and $51 based on earnings prospects and blamed the recent turmoil for hurting investor confidence.

"This is clearly a buying opportunity," Loewen said, predicting a rebound in the stock over the coming six months. "I think we need to get through our year-end and first-quarter (financial reports) and our shareholders will have the comfort they need" to bid the stock up.

His message to Wall Street this week will be that the company is back to its traditional earnings growth rate of about 27 percent a year and as aggressive as ever in making acquisitions. Deals to buy funeral homes and cemeteries should amount to between $600 million and $750 million in 1997, Loewen said.

Given his track record, analysts said it is a good bet that Loewen, a Bible college graduate who grew up on the Canadian prairie, will come out on top. They credit his relentless opposition in the face of the Service threat with causing the Houston giant to reconsider its hostile offer.

Vowing never to succumb, Loewen responded to the bid with a tooth-and-nail defence. It included bringing the antitrust implications of combining the industry's two biggest operators to the attention of regulators and filing an antitrust lawsuit against Service as well.
Loewen owns 956 funeral homes and 313 cemeteries in North America while Service has 2,864 funeral service locations, 335 cemeteries and 147 crematoria worldwide.

Ray Loewen said he felt Service could never have succeeded because, in his opinion, it woefully underestimated the resolve of Loewen management and shareholders and the array of legal and regulatory hurdles to the deal. including the strategic importance of his controlling block of stock in the company.
